This message comes from the UPS Store.
Open this holiday to help with all your small business needs.
Find a store near you at theupsstore.com.
Most locations are independently owned.
Products, services, pricing, and hours of operation may vary.
See Center for details.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
House Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan says he'll help guide Republicans' fight for American families in the new Congress.
NPR's Claudia Grisalei supports Jordan made the remarks after he was elected by his colleagues to the top post.
House Republicans elected Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan leader after House Speaker Mike Johnson said he would step down after last week's midterm election losses.
After the win, Jordan shared some of his plans for the new job.
Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families.
When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom.
And we will bring that fight in committee on the floor and on the stump every single day.
The House Judiciary Committee chair beat the number two House Republican, Steve Scalise, to win the minority leadership role.
Jordan told his colleagues his conference hasn't had a, quote, "clear plan to survive the hour or day in front of us."
But that would change under his leadership. Claudia Grisalei, NPR News.
Among many upsets last week, Democrats flipped a pivotal House seat in California,
as Jackie Fortier with KFF Health News reports Medicaid helped tip the race.
For years, dairy farmer David Valadeo was a Republican voice from California's Central Valley in Congress.
But last week, voters swept him out of office.
Jeff Cummins is a political science professor at California State University, Fresno.
He just had a perfect storm against Valadeo, the national political environment, high inflation, and then his votes in Congress.
Valadeo voted for the big budget bill that cuts Medicaid by more than $900 billion.
He made that decision even though six in 10 people in his district get their health care through Medicaid.
Democrat Randy Villegas was the clear winner. He ran on a platform of universal health care.
That's Jackie Fortier with our partner KFF Health News.
No political leader in the U.S. has made more money while in office than President Trump.
NPR's Rafael Naum explains the two main ways in which Trump has made an estimated nearly $3 billion in his second term.
The first is through the launch of his own meme coin, a cryptocurrency usually based on memes.
According to the president's disclosures, it's earned him over $600 million.
The second is through a crypto company that Trump's family helped start, called World Liberty Financial.
And according to researchers who track his businesses, that netted the president about $1.4 billion.
The president's crypto ventures have attracted a lot of overseas investors, raising concerns they could be trying to court his influence.
The White House strongly denies this, but top Democrats are vowing to take a closer look when they take over Congress next year.
Rafael Naum, NPR News.
U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month in a sign that the rising prices will continue to pose a challenge to Americans.
This is NPR News.
Tennessee is seeking to block Christa Pike's attorneys from accessing the execution drug pentobarbital, used in the 50-year-old inmate's botched execution on the grounds that it would reveal the supplier.
If that happens, the state says it may lose access to the drug and would be unlikely to find an alternative source.
The U.S. is boycotting a key U.N. human rights review for the second year running the only country ever to do so.
The process is a last resort for victims of alleged violations to testify before the U.N.
The Trump administration says the process is biased, as Imogen Folks reports.
U.S. human rights groups led by the American Civil Liberties Union traveled to Geneva with evidence of alleged ill-treatment of migrants and protesters.
U.N. diplomats wanted to ask their U.S. counterparts about the use of the death penalty, restrictions on abortion, and lethal attacks on boats in the Caribbean, viewed by many as illegal.
But Washington was a no-show. The U.S. has already left the U.N. Human Rights Council and says it has no interest in being lectured.
But the review process is not supposed to be optional, and the U.N. now has to decide how to react.
For NPR News, I'm Imogen Folks in Geneva.
When the gales of November came early on this day in 1975, the S.S. Edmund Fitzgerald sank during a storm in Lake Superior.
The ship's tragic sinking claimed the lives of all 29 crew members, who were later memorialized in song by Gordon Lightfoot.
This is NPR.
